sb_prompt: HOW DO YOU FEEL ABOUT THE PRACTICE OF SOME COMPANIES OR GOVERNMENT AGENCIES TESTING EMPLOYEES OR PROSPECTIVE EMPLOYEES FOR DRUGS?  IS RANDOM SPOT TESTING JUSTIFIED?  WHAT LIMITS SHOULD THERE BE?
turns: Yeah, I've just never really bought into the idea of random spot checks myself.

Yeah, I get that skepticism, but honestly, I find the whole thing a lot more complicated than just "privacy." I actually know a guy, Mark, who's a teacher—pretty cool kid, but he got caught up in a program that was supposed to be random, and it wasn't. It felt like fishing. But now that we know there are people out there testing him, well, he's actually doing a lot better than he was before.
That's kind of a heavy thing to go through, though, Mark really shouldn't have had to deal with that kind of fishing?

Yeah, that kind of fishing is brutal, but I think the catch is worth it for him. He's been clean for almost two years now, and honestly, he looked lost before. It feels like the only thing that kept him on the straight and narrow.

I mean, losing yourself like that... yeah, I guess there's something to be said for the threat, but I still can't shake the feeling that you're just punishing people for what they might have done months ago.
I guess that's the whole point though, isn't it? You're not punishing the past, you're making sure they don't drive drunk next Tuesday.
I mean, but if you're punishing the past, how do you know it was even the past you're punishing?

Well, you're right that it feels weird, but once you start digging into the paperwork and the actual testing dates, the "past" thing isn't quite true. It's about catching what's happening *now* before it hits the road or the classroom. If he was caught up *after* a slip-up instead of waiting for a random chance, would he still be here? I don't think so.
I don't know, it still feels a lot like looking back at a mistake rather than stopping it before it happens.
Exactly, look, it feels like looking in the rearview mirror, but honestly, I'm pretty sure you can't see the brake lights if you're just staring straight ahead.
Yeah, but if you're only watching for the brake lights, what's the point of the whole rearview mirror thing?

I mean, maybe I'm just more old-school than you, but I think the point is simple: if you're gonna hire someone to drive your bus or fly your plane, you need to be sure they aren't driving drunk right now. You can't wait for an accident to happen to know.
Right, but what if the person doesn't even know they're being watched? Doesn't that make the whole thing feel like a secret punishment?
That's fair, I guess, but if you keep the blinds up so no one knows you're being watched, how do you expect them to stay sober when they think they're free to drink?
So you're basically saying we should just trust people to make the right choice without supervision?

No, listen, I'm not saying we should just trust them to make the right choice; I'm saying if you don't have the occasional kick in the pants to remind them they're being watched, they'll likely make the wrong one.
Wait, so you're saying he's actually watching him every day just to make sure he doesn't slip up? That's a lot stricter than random testing.

No, I mean, we don't watch him every second like a hawk, but the *threat* is constant. Even if he thinks he got lucky and isn't being tested today, the fact that the system is there and the rules are strict keeps him honest. It's about creating an environment where he *has* to stay clean, not just hoping he will.

Yeah, but if he thinks he got lucky today, does the fact that the system exists actually change his brain chemistry, or is it just him trying to prove he's not a loser to the people who run the program?
Honestly, it's probably half fear and half pride, but the pressure of knowing you're being watched does seem to make people snap out of the fog faster than any advice ever could.
I just don't know if fear can actually fix a brain that's already messed up, or if it just makes people paranoid while the real problem stays underneath.
Look, I'm not saying fear is a magic cure, and I get where you're coming from about the paranoia, but at least it gets him out of the fog long enough to get his life back on track.
I mean, if it's just about keeping him out of the fog for two years, is that a real fix or just a temporary bandage that falls off the second he's alone again?
It might be temporary, but if it's the only thing that got him back on his feet, maybe the bandage is strong enough to hold until he learns how to heal himself?
I guess that's a scary kind of bandage to rely on, though. If you take it off, does the infection just come right back?
Maybe, but look, if the bandage is the only thing holding the wound closed, you've got to keep it on until it heals, right? You don't just yank it off because it looks scary.
Yeah, but once the bandage comes off, how do you know it didn't just let the infection spread again?
That's the whole risk, though—if the bandage stays on too long, he might forget how to walk without it and never learn to heal on his own.
Yeah, but if he never learns how to walk without it, is that really a cure or just another kind of trap?
I mean, maybe the bandage needs to be strong enough to keep the wound closed until he *does* learn to walk on his own, because otherwise, he'll never get there.

Look, I guess that makes sense if he's willing to trade his freedom for his sanity, but it feels like the whole time we're just waiting for him to be ready, and by then he might be too broken to ever be safe again.
You know, I think the problem isn't the testing itself, it's that he never got the chance to heal on his own while it was still on.
Yeah, but if the only way he gets there is by being scared into submission, how do we know he's not just hiding behind the testing program the whole time?
Exactly, but look, if you never test him, he won't ever have to prove he's clean, so he'll probably keep hiding in that dark place until it's too late to fix.

That's a fair point about him never having the chance to heal, but if the testing is the *only* thing holding him back from the dark place, doesn't that mean he never actually had the chance to heal in the first place?
I mean, maybe the test is the only thing that forced him to stop hiding long enough to even *start* the healing process?
So basically, the test is the only thing keeping him from the dark place, but that also means he never really got a chance to heal on his own?
Well, if you take the pressure off too soon, he might just slip back in before he's ready, and then you're right, it's a lost cause.
Yeah, but if he's only clean because he's scared of the test, is he really healed or just really good at hiding it until the test stops?
I guess you're right, maybe he's just playing a really long game of keep-away until the clock runs out.
